meta.title: The Machine in the Back of the Book (sample pages)
meta.author: Ani Kazarian

content: This is the service manual for the Magpie pocket computer. It describes everything the Magpie does, in the order it does it, down to the last number. That is unusual for a manual, so here is why.

If you are reading this, there may not be a Magpie left for you to look at. You won’t need one. Everything a Magpie is lives in these pages, and with this manual and any other computer you can make one.

A Magpie is a set of rules: there are this many numbers in memory, this is what each instruction does to them, this is what the screen shows. The case and the chips only follow them. Anything that follows the rules exactly is a Magpie. A program running on another computer can follow them. When it does, every cartridge made for the Magpie will run on it, and nothing, including the cartridge, can tell the difference.
Owners do not repair. Reduce to 16 pp. owner’s guide (item 9).
A computer. Any computer that will run a program you write: the one on your desk, the one at work, or one that hasn’t been built yet.
Four AA cells, about twenty hours.
Lights when the Magpie stops on something it doesn’t understand. Chapter 4.
Brass, on the underside, engraved with the owner’s name.

content.text: On the underside of every Magpie is a brass plate with its owner’s name on it. The plate is wired to the processor. Instruction 07 reads it: each time the Magpie meets 07 it puts the next letter of the name into A, spaces included, and sets Z as LDA does. After the last letter it gives 0, and the next 07 starts again from the first letter. A Magpie with no name on its plate gives 0 every time. A plate holds up to fourteen letters. A Magpie built on another computer has a plate too: give it the owner’s name when you start it.

content: The underside, with the owner’s plate.
Talin asked if it knew it was hers. It does now.
When you switch on a Magpie with a cartridge in it:
Every byte of memory is set to 0.
The cartridge’s bytes are copied into memory, starting at address $0000.
The registers are set: A to 0, P to 0, S to $FFF0, PC to $0000, and both flags to 0.
With no cartridge in it, the Magpie runs the zeros in its memory. Zero means stop, so it stops at once. That is why a Magpie with no cartridge looks dead.
Magpie Product Group (formerly Magpie Computer Company)
L. R. Garrow, Vice President, Consumer Products

content: Each bit of A stays 1 only if it is 1 in the number too.
Each bit of A becomes 1 if it is 1 in either.
Each bit of A becomes 1 if it is 1 in one but not both.
C := the top bit of A; every bit moves up one; the bottom bit becomes 0.
C := the bottom bit of A; every bit moves down one; the top bit becomes 0.
All five set Z. AND, OR and XOR leave C alone. SHL doubles A and SHR halves it, with the bit that falls off going into C.
AND, OR and XOR leave C alone on purpose. It took me two weeks to decide, and I am not changing it now.
A % in front of a number means it is written in bits.
ADD, SUB, AND, OR, XOR in all three columns.
Z from every one of them; C as the tables say.
